title: Maximum Good Subarray Sum
statement:
You get an integer array `nums` and a positive integer `k`. A contiguous piece `nums[i..j]` counts as **good** when the values at its two ends are exactly `k` apart, that is `|nums[i] - nums[j]| == k`.

Return the largest sum over all good subarrays. The best sum may be negative. If `nums` contains no good subarray at all, return `0`.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every pair of ends costs O(n²). Fix the right end instead: a good subarray ending at value `num` must start at a value equal to `num - k` or `num + k`. Its sum is the running total up to the right end minus the running total just before the start. To make that sum as large as possible, we want the **smallest** "total before" among all earlier positions holding the needed start value. A hash map from value to that smallest total answers this in O(1).

## Approach

1. Keep `prefix`, the sum of the elements seen so far, and `minPrefix`, which maps each value to the smallest `prefix` seen right before any occurrence of it.
2. For each `num`, first record `prefix` (the total before `num`) under `num` if it beats the stored one: `num` may be the start of a later good subarray.
3. Add `num` to `prefix`, so it is now the total through the current position.
4. Look up both possible start values, `num - k` and `num + k`. For each one present, `prefix - minPrefix.get(start)` is the best good sum ending here; keep the maximum in `best`.
5. If `best` never changed, there is no good subarray, so return `0`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`, `k = 1`. Before each value the totals are 0, 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, stored as `1→0, 2→1, 3→3, 4→6, 5→10, 6→15`. At `num = 2`, `prefix = 3` and start `1` gives `3 - 0 = 3`. Then `3` gives `6 - 1 = 5`, `4` gives `10 - 3 = 7`, `5` gives `15 - 6 = 9`, and `6` gives `21 - 10 = 11`. No value `num + 1` appears earlier, so `best = 11`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass with a constant number of map operations per element.
- Space: O(n): the map holds at most one entry per distinct value.

## Pitfalls

- Good sums can be negative, so start `best` at `-Infinity` (not `0`) and convert to `0` only when nothing was found.
- Store the **minimum** prefix for each value, not the first or the last one: a later occurrence can sit after a negative stretch and give a bigger sum.
- Both directions count, because of the absolute value: check `num - k` and `num + k`.
- In Java or C the sums reach about 10^14, so use a 64-bit type.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `minPrefix` | value → smallest total of the elements before any occurrence of that value |
| `prefix` | running sum of the elements processed so far |
| `best` | largest good subarray sum found, `-Infinity` while none exists |
| `num` | the current element, the right end of the subarrays being scored |
| `start` | a value the left end must have: `num - k` or `num + k` |

narration.2: Map each value to the smallest sum of elements standing before one of its occurrences.
narration.3: prefix is the running sum of everything processed so far.
narration.4: No good subarray yet; -Infinity lets a negative good sum still win.
narration.6: Walk the array once, treating each element as the right end of a subarray.
narration.7: Is the total before this element smaller than the one stored for its value?
narration.8: Yes: remember it, because a smaller start total gives a bigger sum later.
narration.10: Include the current element, so prefix now covers everything up to it.
narration.11: A good subarray ending here must start at a value k below or k above num.
narration.12: Has that start value appeared earlier?
narration.13: Its subarray sum is prefix minus the smallest total before that start; keep the best.
narration.17: If nothing good was ever found return 0, otherwise the best sum.
